newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka seeks doctors from Cuba and CIS.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka seeks doctors from Cuba and CIS.

text.p: Sri Lanka is looking to buttress its ailing health sector with doctors from Cuba and the former Soviet Union, Health Minister Mohammed Fowzie said on Sunday.
"We plan to get ... about 60 specialist doctors from Cuba within the next six months," Fowzie told Reuters.

The Ministry of Health is also looking at countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) for an equal number of specialists to serve mostly in rural hospitals where expensive medical equipment is gathering dust due to a lack of qualified doctors, he said.
Sri Lanka has about 6,000 Western-qualified doctors, but only about 400 of them can be termed specialist consultants, ministry sources said. The country has a population of 18 million.
Highly paid specialists also prefer to work in hospitals in and around the capital Colombo, creating a dearth of doctors in outlying areas, they said.
"Quite a lot of our hospitals are equipped to handle surgery, but still we have people dying purely due to surgery being unavailable. We just don't have enough surgeons," Fowzie said.
Affluent Sri Lankan patients travel to India for most types of heart surgery and for some orthopaedic and general surgery, according to hospital sources.
Fowzie said the Cuban specialists would be placed on a two-year contract and paid an allowance of $600 (34,800 rupees) per month in addition to free housing.
"They will be posted to any hospital where there is a need for their services," he said.

The powerful Government Medical Officers' Association, which represents the majority of state-sector doctors, has protested against previous moves by the government to bring foreign doctors to serve in the state health sector.
"I know they (the association) will again say many things. But I am concerned about patients. I want them to get treatment when it is needed and live another day," Fowzie said.
The Health Ministry says Sri Lanka needs to more than double the country's number of doctors and have many more of them trained as specialists by 2005 in order to provide adequate health care.
